A superhigh ductility is exhibited by the as-extruded Mg–8Er binary alloy and the elongation can reach 44%, which is almost 5 times of that of the as-extruded pure Mg.
First, the remarkable refinement of a-Mg grains. According to the Hall–Petch relationship, a remarkable refinement of a-Mg grains can increase the yield strength of Mg–4Er–4Gd–1Zn alloy obviously.

Second, the formation of SFs. According to the TEM observation by Jian et al. [25], SFs would interact with dislocations under the applied stress, and consequently the blocking of dislocations by SFs and the cutting of SFs by dislocations could result in the increase of strength.
Besides blocking dislocations, SFs are also effective in accumulating dislocations, which would increase strain-hardening rate and help with ductility retention.

Third, the basal slip Schmid factor. The high basal slip Schmid factor of Mg–8Er alloy gives a strong contribution to its high ductility. While the low value of basal slip Schmid factor contributes to the high strength for Mg–4Er–4Gd–1Zn alloy.
According to the G–L theory [5–7], damping capacities of Mg alloys are influenced by the maximum strain amplitude and mainly originate in the movement of dislocations.

the special structure of SFs introduces a large amount of interface and dislocation/cluster interaction [24], which should have large effect on damping capacity, and in turn may play an important role in damping mechanism besides movement of dislocation.
